items.excerpt: 49th ASEAN Summit kicks off in Philippines The 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Summits kicked off Sunday in Manila, the Philippines, as leaders from the bloc discussed energy security, food security and economic cooperation, among other topics. During the opening ceremony, an updated ASEAN emblem was unveiled, as Timor-Leste had joined the regional organization. Meanwhile, Philippine President Ferdinand Romualdez Marcos Jr., also the chair of ASEAN 2026, handed over the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement, signed Saturday by the ministers from ASEAN countries, to ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn. Iran's IRGC says drones hit U.S. air defense radar station in Bahrain Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Sunday that its aerospace force had targeted U.S. air defense radar station in Bahrain in a drone attack in the preceding hours. ... Africa CDC warns of immense challenges over fragile Ebola gains Marking six months since the onset of the ongoing Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak, the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has warned that "immense challenges" have fueled the deadly disease's further spread, particularly in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), as cumulative confirmed cases have surpassed 11,100, with over 5,400 deaths. In a statement issued Sunday, which marked six months since the DRC declared the outbreak on May 15, the Africa CDC said that insecurity "remains one of the greatest obstacles to the response," with over 80 attacks on health care during the past six months. It warned that ongoing conflict, displacement, and movement restrictions have continued to complicate containment efforts. Despite the "significant progresses" made in bringing lifesaving services closer to affected communities, the agency said that an average of 400 to 500 new cases continue to be reported each week in the DRC. As the outbreak further spreads, the agency noted that the virus has expanded from just three health zones in a single province to about 67 health zones across eight of the DRC's provinces.

items.excerpt: # Iran drones hit Bahrain again as US-Iran talks stall ## Summary Iranian drones struck a US base in Bahrain for the second time in three days, ending a lull of about two months and pushing military tension back into stalled US-Iran talks.⁠ 1 2 Bahrain issued its first threat alerts since September, with sirens sounding and authorities urging residents to seek shelter after the Revolutionary Guards claimed an attack on a US base.⁠ 2 3 In the Strait of Hormuz, the Revolutionary Guards said two oil tankers caught fire after striking mines.⁠ 4 Trump has reportedly told senior advisers that he may hold off on attacking Iran unless Tehran provokes the United States, which leaves the timing of any renewed strikes open.⁠ 5 In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ebola cases have surpassed 11,000, and the WHO says an armed attack in Cantine-Aloya killed 66 civilians, including three health workers.⁠ 6 Estonia will close all its border crossings with Russia from 1 December, after stopping what it describes as an arson attempt by Russia's GRU military intelligence on a drone factory.⁠ 7 The next test for the US-Iran standoff is whether attacks in Bahrain and Hormuz stop around the Thursday, 19 November, summit in Shenzhen, where Moscow has confirmed a meeting of Trump, Xi and Putin but Beijing has not yet done so.⁠ 1 8

items.title: Fed 'has some work to do on inflation,' Kansas City Fed chief says
items.excerpt: Published Sun, Nov 15 2026 1:58 PM EST Updated Sun, Nov 15 2026 2:04 PM EST ... The Federal Reserve has the tools and responsibility to address price pressures that are "running too hot," and the central bank "has some work to do on inflation," Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid said Sunday. Schmid, speaking to a credit union conference in Hawaii, did not specifically call for additional rate hikes, but said inflation is "uncomfortably above the 2% price stability target, and moving in the wrong direction." Common narratives that have recently evolved around the nature of current inflation and the Fed's ability to contain it are off-base, Schmid said. First, Schmid said, the view that high inflation is a reflection of repeated supply shocks neglects that "inflation is always the result of an imbalance between supply and demand. It is in the context of strong demand that a disruption to supply drives up prices. Demand always plays a role in inflation, and the Fed, through its influence on demand, always has the tools and responsibility to address inflation." Schmid, who is not a Federal Open Market Committee voting member this year, said he also disagrees with the narrative that the sources of demand-induced inflation right now — like the artificial intelligence buildout — are resistant to Fed policy. The Fed raised rates by a quarter-percentage point in September to 3.75%-4.00% but opted not to lift them again at last month's meeting. After recent inflation readings came in higher than expected and comments from other Fed officials, including influential Governor Christopher Waller, interest rate futures markets are now fully priced for a quarter-point increase at December's meeting, with a small probability of a half-point hike. "I would also push back on the idea that meeting our inflation objective requires a reaction from any particular set of prices, for example prices for AI-related technology goods," Schmid said. "Both narratives — that inflation is being driven by either supply shocks or by demand that is impervious to higher interest rates — have a common core," Schmid said. "Mainly, that inflation is somehow beyond the Fed's power to control. I don't believe this to be true. The Fed does have the tools to address inflation and has the responsibility to achieve price stability. As Chairman (Kevin) Warsh said, we have work to do." ## Fed's Collins: Gradual rate hikes best to manage risk On Saturday, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston President Susan Collins said she supported a steady pace of modest interest rate increases because that path of action better manages economic uncertainties. When it comes to moving monetary policy to a tighter footing, "a steady, gradual path seems appropriate to me at the moment. But I'm open-minded," Collins told reporters at a conference held by her bank on housing issues in Boston. "I do see the risks as two-sided on the real side of the economy," Collins said, with inflation high and gains broadening throughout the economy, while the job market was stable and could accelerate. At the same time, Collins said, there are ongoing risks of more shocks hitting the economy. Furthermore, "it's possible that the rise in medium to longer term rates that we've seen since the beginning of the year may actually weigh on demand more than I'm thinking," and serve as another source of restraint on economic activity, she said. For now, all of that argues against the Fed shifting to a more aggressive pace of rate rises to contain inflation that has overshot the Fed's 2% target for more than five years, Collins said. Collins cautioned that her expectation that the Fed can move gradually "doesn't necessarily mean a particular cadence." She also reiterated that the data flow from recent months has shifted, where the Fed could end up in its current tightening cycle.

items.title: Slicing & Dicing The Fed’s Inflation Problem | Morning Briefing | Yardeni Research
items.excerpt: When inflation is driven by supply shocks, there’s less the Fed can do about it. But today’s inflation is not caused totally by supply shocks, won’t simply snap back to the Fed’s target rate when the shocks dispel, and can be influenced by monetary policy. Today, Elias and Ed share their belief that the inflationary environment changed structurally in the years after the pandemic, in ways that make it more difficult for the Fed to achieve its inflation target. Without being able to influence structurally higher goods inflation as much, the Fed will have to lower services inflation by raising the federal funds rate. We think 50 more basis points will do it. Lower oil prices should help to moderate inflation in the near term;

items.title: ICYMI: Fed’s Jefferson says inflation is the key signal for rates, with PCE still at 3.6%
items.excerpt: Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said the path of inflation, rather than growth or jobs, will be the main guide for future interest rate decisions, as price pressures remain well above the central bank’s 2% target. Speaking at the University of California, San Diego Economic Roundtable on Friday, Jefferson said further policy moves should be decided by carefully weighing trends in the data, the changing outlook and the balance of risks, ANI reported. He described inflation’s trajectory as the more important signal for setting the stance of policy. Figures cited in his speech showed headline personal consumption expenditures inflation at 3.6% in September, with core PCE, which strips out food and energy, at 3.1%. Jefferson said the October inflation data received so far point to price pressures staying well above target. He flagged energy as the main risk. Jefferson said he remains concerned that higher energy prices could lead to a broader and more persistent rise in inflation, noting that the effect is already visible in airfares and transport costs. Strong demand for new technologies is also lifting prices of some goods, including memory chips. By contrast, his assessment of the real economy was steady. Jefferson said labour market conditions have stabilised, with unemployment at 4.1% in October, a level he regards as consistent with maximum employment and expects to hold in the near term. The economy has gained momentum this year, he said, with third-quarter GDP growing at an annualised 3.4%, roughly in line with its potential. Jefferson said he voted with the majority to hold rates at the Federal Open Market Committee’s October meeting. Since then, he said, activity and the labour market have remained broadly solid, while inflation readings have continued to show persistent pressure.

items.title: US Treasuries: Two-year yields headed for biggest weekly jump in two years - Markets - Business Recorder
items.excerpt: Published November 16, 2026 Updated November 16, 2026 04:18am By Reuters NEW YORK: Interest rate-sensitive 2-year Treasury yields are headed for the largest weekly increase in more than two years on Friday, after hotter-than-expected consumer price inflation and hawkish Federal Reserve commentary this week led traders to ramp up bets on faster interest rate increases. Treasury yields briefly dipped on Friday after data showed that producer price inflation was lower than economists expected in October, though it showed the largest annual gain in four years. Yields remain sharply higher on the week as traders see rising odds that the US central bank could hike rates by a larger-than-usual 50 basis points in December, or raise rates by 25 basis points at each of the next three meetings. “Inflation is stubbornly high and the Fed’s going to need to act a little bit quicker and a little bit more aggressively,” said Molly Brooks, US rates strategist at TD Securities. Fed funds futures traders are pricing in a 10 percent chance of a 50-basis-point hike at the Fed’s December 8-9 meeting, compared with zero probability a week ago, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch Tool. The odds of the Fed hiking rates by a cumulative 50 basis points by January have risen to 67 percent, from 16 percent a week ago, while 75 basis points of hikes by March has a 48 percent chance, up from 6 percent a week ago. The 2-year note yield was last up 0.34 basis point at 4.867 percent. It earlier reached 4.892 percent, the highest since October 14, and is headed for the biggest weekly increase since the first week of October 2024. The yield on benchmark US 10-year notes rose 4.64 basis points to 5.149 percent. It reached 5.174 percent, the highest since October 14, and is on track for its biggest weekly rise since the April 2025 “tariff tantrum.” The closely watched yield curve between 2- and 10-year notes steepened to 28 basis points. It reached 21 basis points on Thursday, the flattest level since September 24. Fed Governor Christopher Waller raised the prospect of a larger-than-usual 50-basis-point hike in December when he said on Tuesday that the central bank should consider a half-point increase if the inflation picture worsens. A heavy slate of Fed speakers since then has also bolstered the case that a faster pace of rate hikes may be needed to stem inflation, which has been running above the Fed’s 2 percent annual target for almost six years. Boston Fed President Susan Collins said on Friday that tighter monetary policy is coming because of high inflation, in comments that suggested the US central bank may have to raise interest rates more than she initially expected. San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said that her “bias” is that the central bank will need to increase its policy rate, particularly with services inflation moving in the wrong direction and some signs of inflation persistence. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said that price pressures were building far beyond what could be explained by high oil prices, contradicting comments by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that the Fed should not hike rates because of inflation driven by an “energy supply shock” tied to the Iran war.

items.excerpt: Battle for young male voters ‌intensifies after US midterm rebuke of Republicans Barely a week after the midterm elections, Democrats are debating how to turn newfound support among young men into a lasting coalition, while Republicans are trying to understand why the group abandoned them so decisively. An estimated 59% of men ages 18 to 29 voted for Democratic US House of Representatives candidates, compared with 37% for Republicans, according to Tufts University's Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement. That marked a sharp reversal ‌from 2024, when AP VoteCast found young men backing President Donald Trump over Democratic nominee Kamala Harris by 14 points, 56% to 42%. ... Trump's judge appointment blitz faces Republican resistance ... items.title: Trump faces rare Republican revolt as party members seek to oust handpicked RNC chief Joe Gruters - The Economic Times
items.excerpt: AP Last Updated: Nov 16, 2026, 07:49:00 AM IST ... New York: A nascent rebellion is underway against President Donald Trump's handpicked chairman at the Republican National Committee, and it's already getting ugly. Some members are calling for a forensic audit of spending decisions, including hair and makeup services for Trump and other officials, as well as the hiring of the daughter of Trump's former chief of staff. Feuding Republicans are leaking emails and opposition research on rival factions. The White House is threatening to cut off fundraising assistance if the rebels don't fall in line. The emerging fight, which will shape the 2028 presidential nominating contest, represents a rare challenge to Trump's dominance, even after the party's worst midterm performance in a generation. Despite the broad losses, Republican leaders across Washington have shown little desire to move past Trump and have largely stood behind his most unpopular policies. But inside the Republican National Committee, an organisation of 168 members elected from every state who oversee the party's national political operation, a small and growing collection of concerned Republicans are backing an attempt to depose Joe Gruters. Trump wants to keep him in charge. The dissidents are rallying behind Kentucky's KC Crosbie, the RNC's second-in-command. She launched her bid just two days after the Nov. 3 election in a letter that drew the fury of both the White House and Gruters' allies. ... Crosbie remains a vocal Trump supporter who backs his "Make America Great Again" agenda, but her opponents view her gambit as a direct challenge to the president and his power. "Our job is to elect Republicans broadly, not to support one man all the time," said RNC member Oscar Brock of Tennessee, who is supporting Crosbie's candidacy. He said that requires a change in leadership because "there's so much frustration that Chairman Gruters didn't pull his weight in this election." In her letter, Crosbie described the midterms as "a serious setback" and called for the RNC to provide "an honest account" of what went wrong. Crosbie declined to be interviewed. The leadership election will be held in January at the RNC's winter meeting in Arizona. ... Some would-be Crosbie supporters privately acknowledge they're worried about a backlash from the White House, especially with Stephen Miller taking over as Trump's chief of staff. ... Sue Cienki, an RNC committee member from Rhode Island, predicted that Crosbie would have the backing of at least two members from 10 states - a total of 20 - at the committee's January meeting. That's the minimum required for a successful nomination. ... Trump and senior White House officials were livid about Crosbie's Nov 5 letter and the fact that they were given no heads-up. The president soon released a lengthy statement on his Truth Social social media platform hailing Gruters as a "MAGA Warrior" and giving him his "Complete and Total Endorsement." ... The opposition to Gruters has focused on the RNC's spending decisions under him. Republicans had a massive fundraising advantage and still had deep losses. ... In a letter to RNC members sent Thursday night and obtained by The Associated Press, Gruters acknowledged concerns about spending and other issues.

President Donald Trump’s net approval rating improved 3 percentage points over the past week, with 46% approving and 51% disapproving in our latest tracker update. That improvement comes as the federal government’s Oct. 1 shutdown remains our most salient story for the third week in a row. It’s just the latest indication that, as we get into more below, the impasse on Capitol Hill may be full of sound and fury, but signifies nothing for the average voter. ... Just over a third of voters said Trump should prioritize deportations of undocumented immigrants, in line with our findings since before his militarized campaign against illegal immigration in major cities began in August as his approval rating on the matter has rebounded from ... Shutdown Trump is set to host Senate Republicans for lunch at the White House today “to celebrate their unity in the government shutdown fight and for passing nominees,” according to Politico, which noted that the party’s push for a Nov. 21 funding extension may need to change as Washington gets closer to the expiration date. Some conservatives are said to be pushing for a continuing resolution that would run until March or even next October, though the idea irks Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine). Perhaps most notably: NOTUS reports that some Republican senators — even Collins herself — are beginning to entertain the idea of employing the nuclear option to pass a continuing resolution with a simple majority. On the Obamacare front, Politico also reports that Republicans are ramping up talks with the White House on what kind of premium tax credit expansion the party could support once the government is reopened. The party is said to be considering a year-end health care policy package with a two-year extension of scaled-back ACA subsidies though it’s uncertain how that would be received in the House. Nominees The New York Times reports that Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is among at least four Republican senators who have come out in opposition to Trump’s nomination of Paul Ingrassia to lead the Office of Special Counsel following a Politico report documenting a series of racist text messages. That’s enough Republicans to kill Ingrassia’s nomination even before his planned testimony to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday. Separately, Axios noted that Trump has paused the nomination of former Florida Deputy Attorney General John Guard to fill an open open judicial seat in the Middle District of Florida over his connection with a criminal probe, and The Wall Street Journal points out a “power struggle” between Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Elon Musk-aligned billionaire Jared Isaacman over the stewardship of NASA. Gerrymandering House Democratic leaders in Washington have devised a new congressional boundary map for Illinois that would target Republican Rep. Darin LaHood, aiming to reduce the state’s GOP-leaning districts to two, Punchbowl News reports on the party’s response to GOP gerrymandering efforts. Legislators will be in a veto session next week, but will have to move fast ahead of Illinois' pending filing deadline or move next year’s primary date.

items.title: Johnny Depp comeback movie ‘Ebenezer’ lights up box office
items.excerpt: Ryan Coleman November 15, 2026 8:02 p.m. ET ... - Ebenezer topped the box office with $19 million domestically and $42 million globally its premiere weekend. - Ti West’s gothic Christmas parable has courted controversy as the comeback of embattled Johnny Depp. - The Cat in the Hat, Ramayana, and Godzilla Minus Zero all tailed behind, while The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is set up for a big debut next weekend. ... Ebenezer, a new comic-gothic riff on Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol, enjoyed a merry first weekend at the box office. The unlikely duo of stalwart indie director Ti West and controversial star Johnny Depp snagged the No. 1 spot on both the domestic and global leaderboards with $19 million and and $42 million, respectively, per box office tracker Rentrak. Critics may have all but eviscerated the film, but Ebenezer continues the trend of a booming box office reported throughout most of 2026. This weekend marked a 14.2 percent increase in total domestic grosses over the same time last year, when films like Now You See Me: Now You Don’t, The Running Man, and Predator: Badlands duked it out for the top spot. ... However, this weekend’s total gross of $86.8 million marks a 28.5 percent decrease from last weekend. And while Paramount’s Ebenezer cleared its reported $38 million budget, there’s still a long way to go when factoring in marketing and promotional figures, which are routinely excluded from budgetary estimates. With weekend 2 grosses frequently dropping 50 percent or more, and with Ebenezer’s critical notices where they are, the film may struggle to achieve true profitability. The No. 2 and 3 spots on the domestic leaderboard, both in their second weekends, paint a haunting portrait of Ebenezer’s potential future. Warner Bros.’ The Cat in the Hat took the silver medal with just $11.4 million, dropping 42 percent from its $20.5 million open. Then there’s Godzilla Minus Zero. GKids’ CGI spectacular had high ambitions after 2023’s Godzilla Minus One over-performed at the box office. But the sequel dropped a staggering 73 percent in its second weekend in American theaters, earning just $8.3 million. Globally, its haul has reached $89.9 million — far more than necessary to clear its estimated budget of $15 million. But should Ebenezer follow the same path, the eventual result may not be so pretty. Elsewhere, Sony’s Ghost Soldier flopped with a $5.2 million domestic premiere atop its $18 million estimated budget. Amazon’s star-studded How to Rob a Bank, featuring Nicolas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz, and Pete Davidson, earned $5.1 million in its own domestic premiere, an even more dismal open given its estimated budget range of $40-60 million.
